claim: Myofibrils consist of arrays of sarcomeres, the smallest contractile unit of muscles.
source: They consist of arrays of sarcomeres, the smallest contractile unit of muscles.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in muscle biology supported by scientific consensus.

claim: Within a muscle type, myofibril diameter is highly invariant and contributes to its physiological properties.
source: Within a muscle type, myofibril diameter is highly invariant and contributes to its physiological properties, yet little is known about the underlying mechanisms setting myofibril diameter.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Little is known about the underlying mechanisms setting myofibril diameter.
source: Within a muscle type, myofibril diameter is highly invariant and contributes to its physiological properties, yet little is known about the underlying mechanisms setting myofibril diameter.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Zasp is a PDZ and LIM domain protein that is a structural component of Z-discs.
source: Here we show that the PDZ and LIM domain protein Zasp, a structural component of Z-discs, mediates Z-disc and thereby myofibril growth through protein oligomerization.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about Zasp protein structure and localization.

claim: Zasp mediates Z-disc and thereby myofibril growth through protein oligomerization.
source: Here we show that the PDZ and LIM domain protein Zasp, a structural component of Z-discs, mediates Z-disc and thereby myofibril growth through protein oligomerization.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oligomerization of Zasp is induced by an interaction of its ZM domain with LIM domains.
source: Oligomerization is induced by an interaction of its ZM domain with LIM domains.
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data and BiFC assays shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Oligomerization is terminated upon upregulation of shorter Zasp isoforms which lack LIM domains at later developmental stages.
source: Oligomerization is terminated upon upregulation of shorter Zasp isoforms which lack LIM domains at later developmental stages.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data showing temporal expression patterns in Figure 5B.

claim: The balance between growing and blocking isoforms sets the stereotyped diameter of myofibrils.
source: The balance between these two isoforms, which we call growing and blocking isoforms sets the stereotyped diameter of myofibrils.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by multiple experiments including overexpression and mutant analyses.

claim: If blocking isoforms dominate, myofibrils become smaller.
source: If blocking isoforms dominate, myofibrils become smaller.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6 showing smaller Z-discs upon overexpression of blocking isoforms.

claim: If growing isoforms dominate, myofibrils and Z-discs enlarge, eventually resulting in large pathological aggregates that disrupt muscle function.
source: If growing isoforms dominate, myofibrils and Z-discs enlarge, eventually resulting in large pathological aggregates that disrupt muscle function.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1 and 7 showing aggregates and enlarged Z-discs.

claim: Myofibrils are highly organized assemblies of cytoskeletal proteins forming an array of sarcomeres that are embedded in the cytosol of myotubes and mediate contractility.
source: Myofibrils are highly organized assemblies of cytoskeletal proteins forming an array of sarcomeres that are embedded in the cytosol of myotubes and mediate contractility (Huxley and Niedergerke, 1954b; Huxley and Hanson, 1954a; Huxley, 2004; Lemke and Schnorrer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Sarcomeres are composed of actin-containing thin filaments and myosin-containing thick filaments arranged into antiparallel cables.
source: Sarcomeres are composed of actin-containing thin filaments and myosin-containing thick filaments arranged into antiparallel cables.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sarcomere structure.

claim: Thin filaments are anchored to a large multiprotein complex called the Z-disc.
source: Thin filaments are anchored to a large multiprotein complex called the Z-disc (Luther, 2009), and thick filaments are anchored to another large multiprotein complex called the M-line (Agarkova and Perriard, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Thick filaments are anchored to another large multiprotein complex called the M-line.
source: Thin filaments are anchored to a large multiprotein complex called the Z-disc (Luther, 2009), and thick filaments are anchored to another large multiprotein complex called the M-line (Agarkova and Perriard, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Anchoring of myofibrils to the exoskeleton provides the mechanical tension that aligns sarcomeres into myofibrils and coordinates their development.
source: Anchoring of myofibrils to the exoskeleton provides the mechanical tension that aligns sarcomeres into myofibrils and coordinates their development (Weitkunat et al., 2017; Weitkunat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Once aligned, sarcomeres grow to their final size.
source: Once aligned, sarcomeres grow to their final size (Lemke and Schnorrer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Sarcomeres form initially from small structures called Z-bodies that grow eventually into mature Z-discs to which thin filaments are anchored.
source: Electron and confocal microscopy studies showed that sarcomeres form initially from small structures called Z-bodies that grow eventually into mature Z-discs to which thin filaments are anchored (Loison et al., 2018; Orfanos et al., 2015; Reedy and Beall, 1993; Shafiq, 1963; Sparrow and Schöck, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous microscopy studies.

claim: The size of the Z-disc sets the diameter of the myofibril.
source: The size of the Z-disc therefore sets the diameter of the myofibril (Agarkova and Perriard, 2005; Luther, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Z-disc growth and growth termination is poorly understood.
source: While mechanisms have been proposed that set the length of sarcomeres (Fernandes and Schöck, 2014; Gokhin and Fowler, 2013; Tskhovrebova and Trinick, 2017), Z-disc growth and growth termination is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A hallmark of genetically caused myopathies is the appearance of large aggregates composed mainly of Z-disc proteins.
source: A hallmark of genetically caused myopathies is the appearance of large aggregates composed mainly of Z-disc proteins (Kley et al., 2016; Maerkens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on myopathies.

claim: Many myopathy-associated mutations encode Z-disc proteins.
source: Interestingly, many myopathy-associated mutations encode Z-disc proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the myopathy field.

claim: Mutations in any of the four α-actinin genes or in Zasp and other Alp/Enigma family genes in humans cause myopathies characterized by the presence of large aggregates.
source: Mutations in any of the four α-actinin genes or in Zasp and other Alp/Enigma family genes in humans cause myopathies characterized by the presence of large aggregates (Murphy and Young, 2015; Selcen and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous clinical and genetic studies.

claim: The aggregation phenotype is conserved among animals: fruit flies with mutations in myopathy-related genes also develop Z-disc aggregates.
source: The aggregation phenotype is conserved among animals: fruit flies with mutations in myopathy-related genes also develop Z-disc aggregates (González-Morales et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: α-Actinin and Zasp are conserved proteins that coordinate Z-disc formation.
source: α-Actinin and Z-disc Alternatively Spliced Protein (Zasp) are conserved proteins that coordinate Z-disc formation (Faulkner et al., 1999; Katzemich et al., 2013; Murphy and Young, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: α-Actinin forms a rod-shaped antiparallel homodimer at the Z-disc, where it crosslinks and serves as an attachment point for actin filaments.
source: α-Actinin forms a rod-shaped antiparallel homodimer at the Z-disc, where it crosslinks and serves as an attachment point for actin filaments (Djinović-Carugo et al., 1999; Luther, 2009; Murphy and Young, 2015; Ribeiro et al., 2014; Rusu et al., 2017; Takahashi and Hattori, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural and functional studies.

claim: Zasp and other members of the Alp/Enigma family of proteins are scaffolding proteins with an α-actinin-binding PDZ domain, an uncharacterized Zasp Motif (ZM) domain, and one to four protein-protein interaction LIM domains.
source: Zasp and other members of the Alp/Enigma family of proteins are scaffolding proteins with an α-actinin-binding PDZ domain (InterPro: IPR001478), an uncharacterized Zasp Motif (ZM; InterPro: IPR031847 and IPR006643) domain, and one to four protein-protein interaction LIM domains (InterPro: IPR001781) (Finn et al., 2017; Klaavuniemi et al., 2004; Liao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and protein domain databases.

claim: Zasp and α-actinin proteins are present at the earliest stages of Z-disc formation, and are required for Z-disc assembly.
source: Zasp and α-actinin proteins are present at the earliest stages of Z-disc formation, and are required for Z-disc assembly (Dabiri et al., 1997; Katzemich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Vertebrates have seven Alp/Enigma genes, each encoding several isoforms.
source: Vertebrates have seven Alp/Enigma genes, each encoding several isoforms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate gene families.

claim: The Drosophila genome has three Zasp genes, Zasp52, Zasp66, and Zasp67, which encode 21, 12, and 4 isoforms, respectively.
source: The Drosophila genome has three Zasp genes, Zasp52, Zasp66, and Zasp67, which encode 21, 12, and 4 isoforms, respectively (Gramates et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to FlyBase database.

claim: Zasp66 and Zasp67 are duplications of Zasp52 and resemble the smallest isoforms of Zasp52.
source: Zasp66 and Zasp67 are duplications of Zasp52 and resemble the smallest isoforms of Zasp52 (González-Morales et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Overexpression of full-length Zasp52-PR transgene in the indirect flight muscles of adult flies causes formation of large aggregates.
source: To examine if this holds true in Drosophila, we overexpressed a full-length Zasp52-PR transgene consisting of a PDZ, a ZM, and 4 LIM domains in the indirect flight muscles (IFM) of adult flies, which causes formation of large aggregates (Figure 1A,B,I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The absence of LIM domains (Zasp52-PP) abolishes aggregate formation.
source: To determine which domain is responsible for aggregation, we deleted them individually: the absence of LIM domains (Zasp52-PP) and ZM domain (Zasp52-PR∆ZM) abolished aggregate formation, whereas removal of the PDZ domain only slightly reduced the number of aggregates (Zasp52-PR∆PDZ, Figure 1C–E,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Deletion of the ZM domain (Zasp52-PR∆ZM) abolishes aggregate formation.
source: To determine which domain is responsible for aggregation, we deleted them individually: the absence of LIM domains (Zasp52-PP) and ZM domain (Zasp52-PR∆ZM) abolished aggregate formation, whereas removal of the PDZ domain only slightly reduced the number of aggregates (Zasp52-PR∆PDZ, Figure 1C–E,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Removal of the PDZ domain only slightly reduces the number of aggregates.
source: To determine which domain is responsible for aggregation, we deleted them individually: the absence of LIM domains (Zasp52-PP) and ZM domain (Zasp52-PR∆ZM) abolished aggregate formation, whereas removal of the PDZ domain only slightly reduced the number of aggregates (Zasp52-PR∆PDZ, Figure 1C–E,I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The PDZ domain is required for binding α-actinin, a crucial crosslinker of actin filaments at the Z-disc.
source: The PDZ domain is required for binding α-actinin, a crucial crosslinker of actin filaments at the Z-disc (Katzemich et al., 2013; Liao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reducing α-actinin levels by RNAi in Zasp52-PR overexpression reduces aggregate formation to a similar level as PDZ deletion.
source: Reducing α-actinin levels by RNAi in Zasp52-PR overexpression reduces aggregate formation to a similar level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that α-actinin increases aggregate number, but is not required for their initial formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: α-actinin increases aggregate number, but is not required for their initial formation.
source: Reducing α-actinin levels by RNAi in Zasp52-PR overexpression reduces aggregate formation to a similar level (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that α-actinin increases aggregate number, but is not required for their initial formation.
evidence: This is an inference from the RNAi experiment data.

claim: Expression of the paralogous genes Zasp66 and Zasp67, which lack LIM domains like Zasp52-PP, does not result in aggregate formation.
source: Expression of the paralogous genes Zasp66 and Zasp67 (González-Morales et al., 2019), which lack LIM domains like Zasp52-PP, also does not result in aggregate formation (Figure 1F,G and I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Overexpression of Zasp52-PK consisting of PDZ, ZM and 1 LIM domain does not form aggregates.
source: Finally, we tested if multiple LIM domains are required for aggregate formation by overexpressing Zasp52-PK consisting of PDZ, ZM and 1 LIM domain. No aggregates form (Figure 1H and I) indicating that the ZM domain and multiple LIM domains are required for aggregate formation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The ZM domain and multiple LIM domains are required for aggregate formation.
source: Finally, we tested if multiple LIM domains are required for aggregate formation by overexpressing Zasp52-PK consisting of PDZ, ZM and 1 LIM domain. No aggregates form (Figure 1H and I) indicating that the ZM domain and multiple LIM domains are required for aggregate formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Mild overexpression of Zasp52-PR using UH3-Gal4 results in Z-discs that are bigger than the control, but aggregates are not present.
source: To test if aggregates formed as a result of Z-disc overgrowth, we tested the overexpression of Zasp52-PR using UH3-Gal4, a driver line that has the same temporal and spatial expression pattern as Act88-Gal4 but is expressed at a much lower level. To better capture the size variation, we measured the Z-disc height that corresponds to the disc diameter and categorized them into specific size categories. In this condition, Z-discs are bigger than the control, but aggregates are not present (Figure 1J–L), indicating that Z-disc growth and pathological aggregation correlate with the amount of Zasp52 protein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J-L.

claim: Z-disc growth and pathological aggregation correlate with the amount of Zasp52 protein.
source: In this condition, Z-discs are bigger than the control, but aggregates are not present (Figure 1J–L), indicating that Z-disc growth and pathological aggregation correlate with the amount of Zasp52 protein.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the dose-dependent effects observed in the experiments.

claim: Zasp52-PK and Zasp52-PE can interact with each other in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: Zasp52-PK and Zasp52-PE, another full-length isoform, can interact with each other, whereas controls do not interact (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Full-length isoforms of Zasp66 and Zasp67 (Zasp66-PK and Zasp67-PD) can interact with Zasp52-PK and Zasp52-PE.
source: Full-length isoforms of Zasp66 and Zasp67 (Zasp66-PK and Zasp67-PD) can also interact with Zasp52-PK and Zasp52-PE (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Zasp proteins can homo- and heterodimerize.
source: These data suggest that Zasp proteins can homo- and heterodimerize.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the yeast two-hybrid interaction data.

claim: Flag-tagged Zasp52 co-immunoprecipitates with GFP-tagged Zasp52 from thorax muscle extracts.
source: We confirmed these results by co-immunoprecipitation of Flag-tagged Zasp52 with GFP-tagged Zasp52 from thorax muscle extracts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bacterially purified His-Zasp52-PK-Flag dimerizes in vitro in a chemical crosslinking assay.
source: Furthermore, bacterially purified His-Zasp52-PK-Flag dimerized in vitro in a chemical crosslinking assay (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by crosslinking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Zasp52-PK interacts with the ZM domain and LIM domains.
source: Zasp52-PK interacts with the ZM domain and LIM domains, whereas Zasp66 and Zasp67 only interact with LIM domains (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Zasp66 and Zasp67 only interact with LIM domains.
source: Zasp52-PK interacts with the ZM domain and LIM domains, whereas Zasp66 and Zasp67 only interact with LIM domains (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Dimerization is mediated by a ZM-LIM domain interaction.
source: This suggests that dimerization is mediated by a ZM-LIM domain interaction, and because Zasp66 and Zasp67 lack LIM domains, they cannot interact with the ZM domain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the domain interaction data.

claim: Zasp66 and Zasp67 cannot interact with the ZM domain because they lack LIM domains.
source: This suggests that dimerization is mediated by a ZM-LIM domain interaction, and because Zasp66 and Zasp67 lack LIM domains, they cannot interact with the ZM domain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the domain composition and interaction data.

claim: When the ZM domain of Zasp66 is deleted, the interaction with LIM domains is abolished.
source: To confirm this hypothesis, we next tested the interaction of LIM2A, LIM2B, LIM3 and Zasp52-PK with a series of Zasp66 deletion constructs. As soon as the ZM domain of Zasp66 is deleted, the interaction with LIM domains is abolished (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by yeast two-hybrid data with deletion constructs shown in Figure 2D.

claim: LIM-ZM binding mediates homo- and heterodimerization between Zasp proteins.
source: Thus, LIM-ZM binding mediates homo- and heterodimerization between Zasp proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the comprehensive domain interaction mapping experiments.

claim: Zasp66-GFP fluorescence is mildly reduced in Zasp52MI02988 mutants.
source: Zasp66-GFP fluorescence is mildly reduced in Zasp52MI02988 mutants (Figure 3A,B and D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Zasp66-GFP fluorescence is strongly reduced in Zasp52MI00979 mutants.
source: In contrast, Zasp66-GFP fluorescence is strongly reduced in Zasp52MI00979 mutants (Figure 3C and D), suggesting that Zasp52 recruits other Zasp proteins through its LIM domains, consistent with the Y2H results.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Zasp52 recruits other Zasp proteins through its LIM domains.
source: In contrast, Zasp66-GFP fluorescence is strongly reduced in Zasp52MI00979 mutants (Figure 3C and D), suggesting that Zasp52 recruits other Zasp proteins through its LIM domains, consistent with the Y2H results.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Zasp52 mutants on Zasp66 localization.

claim: α-Actinin localization at the Z-disc was not decreased in any of the Zasp mutants.
source: α-Actinin localization at the Z-disc was not decreased in any of the Zasp mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zasp52-PK-NYFP and Zasp52-PK-CYFP show specific fluorescence at the Z-disc in BiFC assays.
source: Zasp52-PK-NYFP and Zasp52-PK-CYFP show specific fluorescence at the Z-disc, whereas controls do not (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: This is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ZM-only isoform Zasp66-PH-NYFP interacts specifically with Zasp52-PK-CYFP at the Z-disc.
source: More importantly, the ZM-only isoform Zasp66-PH-NYFP interacts specifically with Zasp52-PK-CYFP at the Z-disc (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by BiFC data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: ZM-LIM interaction of Zasp proteins occurs in vivo at the Z-disc.
source: Thus, ZM-LIM interaction of Zasp proteins occurs in vivo at the Z-disc.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the BiFC experiments demonstrating interaction in living tissue.

claim: LIM domains are well-known protein-protein interaction domains.
source: LIM domains are well-known protein-protein interaction domains (Kadrmas and Beckerle, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Functional information on the ZM domain is scarce.
source: In contrast, functional information on the ZM domain is scarce.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The ZM domain is an uncharacterized short motif of 26 amino acids found only in Alp/Enigma proteins.
source: It is an uncharacterized short motif of 26 amino acids found only in Alp/Enigma proteins (Klaavuniemi et al., 2004; Letunic et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and protein domain databases.

claim: Alignment of Drosophila Zasp-encoding genes to the ZM consensus sequence shows weak conservation.
source: Alignment of Drosophila Zasp-encoding genes to the ZM consensus sequence shows weak conservation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The ZM domain is only present in a subset of animal genomes and absent from plants, fungi and unicellular metazoans.
source: In contrast to the universal presence of LIM domains in eukaryotes, the ZM domain is only present in a subset of animal genomes and absent from plants, fungi and unicellular metazoans (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B using PFAM database data.

claim: Muscle striation evolved independently in cnidarians and bilaterians, with only the latter showing a canonical Z-disc structure.
source: Muscle striation evolved independently in cnidarians and bilaterians, with only the latter showing a canonical Z-disc structure (Steinmetz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous evolutionary study.

claim: The ZM domain is restricted to bilateral animals.
source: Intriguingly, the ZM domain is restricted to bilateral animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic distribution data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Canonical Z-discs and ZM domains arose together during evolution.
source: Thus, our correlative data suggest that canonical Z-discs and ZM domains arose together during evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the correlation between ZM domain presence and canonical Z-disc structure.

claim: Growing isoforms are overrepresented at earlier stages of Z-disc formation, and blocking isoforms at later stages.
source: To regulate Z-disc growth, growing isoforms should be overrepresented at earlier stages of Z-disc formation, and blocking isoforms at later stages, to stop Z-disc growth.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain Z-disc growth regulation.

claim: Multivalent Zasp52 growing isoforms are already strongly expressed at 24 hr APF, whereas some blocking isoforms without any LIM domains are expressed only after 60 hr APF.
source: We observed earlier expression of the growing isoforms compared to the blocking isoforms (Figure 5B). For example, multivalent Zasp52 growing isoforms are already strongly expressed at 24 hr APF, whereas some blocking isoforms without any LIM domains are expressed only after 60 hr APF (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Z-discs grow at the periphery of the disc, starting as a small Z-body.
source: Z-discs grow at the periphery of the disc, starting as a small Z-body (Orfanos et al., 2015; Shwartz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Growing isoforms are enriched at the centre and blocking isoforms are enriched at the periphery of the final-sized Z-disc.
source: Our model therefore predicts growing isoforms to be enriched at the centre and blocking isoforms to be enriched at the periphery of the final-sized Z-disc.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that is then tested experimentally.

claim: Actin is evenly distributed in the Z-disc.
source: Actin is evenly distributed in the Z-disc (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by cross-section imaging data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The growing isoforms are present throughout the disc, but most concentrated at the centre of the Z-disc.
source: The growing isoforms are present throughout the disc, but most concentrated at the centre of the Z-disc (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by cross-section imaging data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The blocking isoforms Zasp66 and Zasp67 are partially excluded from the centre of the disc and form a ring-like pattern.
source: The blocking isoforms Zasp66 and Zasp67 are partially excluded from the centre of the disc and form a ring-like pattern (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: This is supported by cross-section imaging data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Zasp66 localizes more at the periphery compared to Zasp67, which correlates with its later expression peak compared to Zasp67.
source: Zasp66 localizes more at the periphery compared to Zasp67, which correlates with its later expression peak compared to Zasp67 (middle panels of Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a correlation observed between localization and expression timing data.

claim: Only the Zasp52MI00979 mutant, which deletes multiple LIM domains, had smaller Z-discs compared to the control.
source: Interestingly, only the Zasp52MI00979 mutant, which deletes multiple LIM domains, had smaller Z-discs compared to the control (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: This is supported by Z-disc size measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: In Zasp52MI00979, the smaller size categories were significantly elevated, whereas Zasp52MI02988 was comparable to the control.
source: In Zasp52MI00979, the smaller size categories were significantly elevated, whereas Zasp52MI02988 was comparable to the control (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by Z-disc size distribution data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Overexpression of the Zasp52-PP blocking isoform led to smaller Z-discs than the control.
source: We next determined if the opposite approach, increasing the levels of blocking isoforms, also results in smaller Z-discs. Overexpressing the Zasp52-PP blocking isoform led to smaller Z-discs than the control (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by Z-disc size measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The small Z-disc effect of Zasp52-PP overexpression requires the ZM domain.
source: This effect requires the ZM domain, because overexpression of Zasp52-Stop143 containing only a functional extended PDZ domain, causes a milder phenotype than Zasp52-PP (Figure 6D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of phenotypes from different construct overexpressions.

claim: Overexpression of Zasp66 or Zasp67 resulted in smaller Z-discs.
source: Like Zasp52-PP, overexpression of Zasp66 or Zasp67 resulted in smaller Z-discs (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by Z-disc size measurements shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Upon overexpression of Zasp52-PP, but not of Zasp52-Stop143, Zasp52-mCherry recruitment to the Z-disc is reduced.
source: We also confirmed these phenotypes by measuring the relative fluorescence of Zasp52-mCherry at the Z-disc. Upon overexpression of Zasp52-PP, but not of Zasp52-Stop143, Zasp52-mCherry recruitment to the Z-disc is reduced (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Overexpression of Zasp66 and Zasp67 reduces Zasp52-mCherry recruitment to the Z-disc.
source: Likewise, overexpression of Zasp66 and Zasp67 reduces Zasp52-mCherry recruitment to the Z-disc (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 6G.

claim: α-actinin levels were unchanged in Zasp overexpression conditions.
source: In contrast, α-actinin levels were unchanged in Zasp overexpression conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increasing the ZM/LIM ratio in IFM results in smaller Z-discs.
source: These data indicate that increasing the ZM/LIM ratio in IFM results in smaller Z-discs.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the overexpression experiments.

claim: Rare aggregates are observed in Zasp66 and Zasp67 single mutants.
source: We observed rare aggregates in Zasp66 and Zasp67 single mutants (Figure 7A,B,D).
evidence: This is supported by aggregate frequency data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Frequent aggregates are observed in the Zasp66 Zasp67 double mutant.
source: As these two proteins likely have some redundant roles, we also analyzed the Zasp66 Zasp67 double mutant, where we observed frequent aggregates (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by aggregate frequency data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The Zasp66 Zasp67 double mutant had enlarged Z-discs, whereas the single mutants had normal-sized Z-discs.
source: Additionally, the single mutants had normal-sized Z-discs, whereas the double mutant had enlarged Z-discs (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by Z-disc size measurements shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Blocking isoforms are required to prevent Z-disc overgrowth.
source: Thus, blocking isoforms are required to prevent Z-disc overgrowth.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the Zasp66 Zasp67 double mutant phenotype.

claim: Co-overexpression of both growing and the Zasp52-PP blocking isoform suppressed aggregate formation compared to a LacZ control.
source: Co-overexpression of both growing and the Zasp52-PP blocking isoform suppressed aggregate formation compared to a LacZ control (Figure 7F–I).
evidence: This is supported by aggregate frequency data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The mutated blocking isoform Zasp52-Stop143 without the ZM domain did not suppress aggregation.
source: The mutated blocking isoform Zasp52-Stop143 without the ZM domain did not suppress aggregation (Figure 7H,I).
evidence: This is supported by aggregate frequency data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Co-overexpression of Zasp66 or Zasp67 suppressed aggregation.
source: Co-overexpression of Zasp66 or Zasp67 also suppressed aggregation (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by aggregate frequency data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Z-disc formation and growth is driven by multivalent oligomerization of Zasp proteins with multiple LIM domains.
source: Our findings indicate that Z-disc formation and growth is driven by multivalent oligomerization of Zasp proteins with multiple LIM domains, and eventually terminated at the proper Z-disc size by the upregulation of blocking isoforms without LIM domains (see model in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study synthesizing all experimental findings.

claim: Z-disc growth is eventually terminated at the proper Z-disc size by the upregulation of blocking isoforms without LIM domains.
source: Our findings indicate that Z-disc formation and growth is driven by multivalent oligomerization of Zasp proteins with multiple LIM domains, and eventually terminated at the proper Z-disc size by the upregulation of blocking isoforms without LIM domains (see model in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study synthesizing all experimental findings.

claim: The process of Z body and Z-disc formation is reminiscent of membraneless organelles with compositions distinct from the surrounding cytosol, which form through a mechanism of phase separation.
source: The process of Z body and Z-disc formation is reminiscent of membraneless organelles with compositions distinct from the surrounding cytosol, which form through a mechanism of phase separation (e.g. Cajal bodies or P bodies) (Boeynaems et al., 2018; Weber, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative comparison to other cellular structures supported by citations.

claim: Both Z-discs and membraneless organelles have sharp boundaries between themselves and the cytoplasm, they form and organize as discrete puncta in the cytosol, and multivalent protein domains are often involved in their formation.
source: Both have sharp boundaries between themselves and the cytoplasm, they form and organize as discrete puncta in the cytosol, and multivalent protein domains are often involved in their formation (Li et al., 2012; Weber, 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison supported by citations to literature on membraneless organelles.

claim: Sarcomere size is stereotyped in a given muscle type but distinct among different muscles.
source: Sarcomere size is stereotyped in a given muscle type but distinct among different muscles (Schönbauer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The sarcomere grows while the Zasp growing isoforms dominate the Zasp isoform pool.
source: The sarcomere grows, while the Zasp growing isoforms dominate the Zasp isoform pool.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model proposed in the study.

claim: Different sarcomere sizes can be achieved by varying the sarcomere growth period or the speed at which new Zasp molecules are recruited to the Z-disc.
source: Different sarcomere sizes can be achieved in two ways. First, the sarcomere growth period – the window of time in which Zasp growing isoforms dominate, might vary among muscle types. Second, the speed at which new Zasp molecules are recruited to the Z-disc, might be different among muscle types, while the growth period remains constant.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for how the mechanism could account for size variation.

claim: A combination of varying growth period and recruitment speed strategies likely occur simultaneously to achieve different sarcomere sizes.
source: Given the diversity of muscle types and therefore sarcomere sizes that exist, it is likely that a combination of these two strategies occur simultaneously.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about mechanisms.

claim: Additional redundant mechanisms to control Z-disc growth might exist, as evidenced by the observation that Zasp52-PR overexpression makes big Z-discs and aggregates, while the mutant removing Zasp52 LIM domains reduces Z-disc size to a comparatively small degree.
source: Finally, apart from the ZM-LIM mechanism described here, additional redundant mechanisms to control Z-disc growth might exist, as evidenced by the observation that Zasp52-PR overexpression makes big Z-discs and aggregates, while the mutant removing Zasp52 LIM domains reduces Z-disc size to a comparatively small degree.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the asymmetry of phenotypes.

claim: Redundant mechanisms might operate through other LIM domain proteins, or the coordination of Z-disc and M-line growth.
source: Redundant mechanisms might operate through other LIM domain proteins, or the coordination of Z-disc and M-line growth, all of which may provide important buffering functions to ensure proper myofibril size, which is crucial for fully functional muscles.
evidence: This is speculation about potential additional mechanisms.

claim: On its own, the ZM domain from two mouse Zasp proteins localizes to the Z-disc.
source: On its own, the ZM domain from two mouse Zasp proteins localizes to the Z-disc (Klaavuniemi et al., 2004; Klaavuniemi and Ylänne, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Z-disc localization is a conserved feature of ZM domains from vertebrates to insects.
source: Our data suggest that Z-disc localization is a conserved feature of ZM domains from vertebrates to insects.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data of Zasp66-PH shown in the study.

claim: ZM-containing proteins are tethered to the Z-disc by the physical interaction with the LIM domains of other Zasp proteins.
source: ZM-containing proteins are tethered to the Z-disc by the physical interaction with the LIM domains of other Zasp proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the interaction and localization studies.

claim: The LIM domain serves as a recruitment signal for Zasp proteins and potentially other unidentified ZM-containing proteins to join the Z-disc.
source: In sum, the LIM domain serves as a recruitment signal for Zasp proteins and potentially other unidentified ZM-containing proteins to join the Z-disc.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study with speculation about other proteins.

claim: A conserved mechanism involving LIM-ZM binding underlies Z-disc growth and growth termination.
source: In addition, given the appearance of the ZM domain in bilateral animals with canonical Z-discs, we postulate that a conserved mechanism involving LIM-ZM binding underlies Z-disc growth and growth termination.
evidence: This is a postulate based on the phylogenetic correlation and experimental data.

claim: In vertebrates, the Zasp proteins are very diverse and are better known as Alp/Enigma family.
source: In vertebrates, the Zasp proteins are very diverse and are better known as Alp/Enigma family: ZASP/Cypher/Oracle/LDB3/PDLIM6, ENH/PDLIM5, PDLIM7/ENIGMA/LMP-1, CLP36/PDLIM1/Elfin/hCLIM1, PDLIM2/Mystique/SLIM, ALP/PDLIM3, and RIL/PDLIM4.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate protein families.

claim: The ZM/DUF4749 motif occurs in ZASP, CLP36, PDLIM2, ALP and RIL.
source: The ZM/DUF4749 motif occurs in ZASP, CLP36, PDLIM2, ALP and RIL (Cheng et al., 2010; D'Cruz et al., 2016; Faulkner et al., 1999; Vallenius et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The LIM domain occurs in all Zasp proteins, either as one domain in Alp family members or as three domains in Enigma family members.
source: The LIM domain occurs in all Zasp proteins, either as one domain in Alp family members or as three domains in Enigma family members (Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Zasp66 and Zasp67 genes are insect-specific.
source: Although Zasp66 and Zasp67 genes are insect-specific (González-Morales et al., 2019), vertebrate Alp/Enigma genes also express isoforms without LIM domains that could fulfill a blocking isoform function (Cheng et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Vertebrate Alp/Enigma genes also express isoforms without LIM domains that could fulfill a blocking isoform function.
source: Although Zasp66 and Zasp67 genes are insect-specific (González-Morales et al., 2019), vertebrate Alp/Enigma genes also express isoforms without LIM domains that could fulfill a blocking isoform function (Cheng et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations showing such isoforms exist.

claim: Because Zasp52-PK, which only contains one LIM domain, behaves as a blocking isoform, the Alp members with only one LIM domain might also behave as blocking isoforms.
source: In addition, because Zasp52-PK, which only contains one LIM domain, behaves as a blocking isoform, the Alp members with only one LIM domain might also behave as blocking isoforms.
evidence: This is speculation based on extrapolation from Drosophila data to vertebrates.

claim: The Enigma family members contain three C-terminal LIM domains, making them ideal candidates to fulfill the growing role in vertebrates.
source: The function of the growing isoforms of Zasp requires multiple functional LIM domains. As the Enigma family members contain three C-terminal LIM domains, they are the ideal candidates to fulfill the growing role in vertebrates.
evidence: This is speculation based on domain composition.

claim: Three Enigma proteins exist in vertebrates: PDLIM7/Enigma/LMP-1, ENH/PDLIM5 and ZASP/Cypher/Oracle/LDB3/PDLIM6.
source: Three Enigma proteins exist in vertebrates: PDLIM7/Enigma/LMP-1, ENH/PDLIM5 and ZASP/Cypher/Oracle/LDB3/PDLIM6.
evidence: This is established knowledge about vertebrate proteins.

claim: Functional redundancy between Enigma proteins at the Z-disc is likely common and demonstrated in one case.
source: Functional redundancy between them at the Z-disc is likely common and demonstrated in one case (Mu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In Cypher knockout mice sarcomere assembly occurs normally during development, followed by immediate sarcomere failure after postnatal onset of contractility.
source: In Cypher knockout mice sarcomere assembly occurs normally during development, followed by immediate sarcomere failure after postnatal onset of contractility (Zhou et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: ENH mutants exhibit cardiac dilation and abnormal Z-disc structure in the heart.
source: ENH mutants exhibit cardiac dilation and abnormal Z-disc structure in the heart (Cheng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In both Cypher and ENH single mutants, as well as Cypher ENH double mutants, sarcomeres look considerably smaller in diameter in electron microscopy images.
source: Intriguingly, in both Cypher and ENH single mutants, as well as Cypher ENH double mutants, sarcomeres look considerably smaller in diameter in electron microscopy images (Cheng et al., 2010; Mu et al., 2015; Zhou et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A similar role for Enigma proteins in setting sarcomere diameter in vertebrates appears likely.
source: Thus, a similar role for Enigma proteins in setting sarcomere diameter in vertebrates appears likely.
evidence: This is speculation based on the phenotypes observed in vertebrate mutants.

claim: Many myopathies present aggregates, and several human ZASP mutations have been linked to aggregate-forming myopathies.
source: Our Z-disc oligomerization hypothesis agrees well with the observation that many myopathies present aggregates, and several human ZASP mutations have been linked to aggregate-forming myopathies (Murphy and Young, 2015; Selcen and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical literature.

claim: Many ZASP mutations linked to disease lie within the ZM domain or one of the LIM domains.
source: Many ZASP mutations linked to disease lie within the ZM domain or one of the LIM domains (Selcen and Engel, 2005; Theis et al., 2006; Vatta et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical and genetic studies.

claim: Protein aggregation in myopathy patients might be a consequence of an imbalance in the mechanism that controls sarcomere size, favoring the growing over the blocking isoforms.
source: Protein aggregation in myopathy patients might be a consequence of an imbalance in the mechanism that controls sarcomere size, favoring the growing over the blocking isoforms.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying human disease.

claim: The data points to a potential therapeutic avenue: blocking the growing isoforms with short peptides containing a ZM domain.
source: If this were the case, our data points to a potential therapeutic avenue: blocking the growing isoforms with short peptides containing a ZM domain.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications.
